title: Improving a policy
objectives: Build policy iteration and check that it reaches value iteration's policy.

screens.title: Can we do better than always up?
screens.prose: On the slippery grid, the policy "always move U" has the values shown, all negative: it often bumps the top edge for ever. At the start, row 4 column 1, it scores −0.3686. Use these values to score moving R there instead, for one step, then following "always U".
screens.question: What does R score at the start? Give a decimal to 4 places.

hints.text: R reaches row 4 column 2 with 0.8; a slip U reaches row 3 column 1; a slip D bumps the edge.
Score: $-0.04 + 0.9 \times$ the average landing value.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Average the three landing values, then score the move.

byKey.sign: Check the sign: every landing value is negative.
byKey.no-slip: You took R as certain. It slips U or D one time in ten each.
byKey.u: That is the score of U, the current policy. The question asks about R.

explain.text: R scores -0.3573 against U's −0.3686, so switching the start to R, and then following the old policy, is better. Making that switch in every cell at once is **policy improvement**.

screens.title: Evaluate, improve, repeat
screens.prose: Policy iteration evaluates the policy exactly, as in l6, switches every cell to its best move under those values, and repeats. Slide through the policies, starting from "always U".
screens.question: How many evaluations does it take before an improvement step changes nothing?

hints.text: Watch the arrows from one policy to the next.
Count the policies until two in a row are the same.

feedback.correct: Four: the fourth policy's improvement changes no arrow.
feedback.generic: Slide to the end and count the policies.

byKey.three: The third policy still has one cell to change.
byKey.five: There are only four policies: the fourth is already stable.
byKey.vi: That is value iteration's sweep count. Policy iteration takes far fewer, bigger steps.

explain.text: The policies change 13, 5 and 1 cells, then none. The 4 evaluations reach the same policy value iteration found, against 25 sweeps. Each evaluation costs a linear solve, though.

screens.title: Never worse
screens.prose: **Policy improvement**: given $v_\pi$, choose in every state the action with the best one-step score, $\pi'(s) = \arg\max_a \sum_{s'} p\,[r + \gamma v_\pi(s')]$. The **policy improvement theorem** says $v_{\pi'}(s) \ge v_\pi(s)$ in every state.
screens.question: By how much did the first improvement raise the start's value? Give a decimal to 3 places.

hints.text: Before: −0.3686. After: read the start cell.
After the first improvement the start is worth 0.0845.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract the old value from the new one.

byKey.new: That is the new value. The rise is new minus old.
byKey.sum: You subtracted 0.3686 instead of adding: the old value is negative.
byKey.one-step: That is the gain from changing only the start's first move. Every cell changed, and the gains compound.

explain.text: The start rose from −0.3686 to 0.0845, by 0.453. Changing one move alone gained only 0.0113; improving every cell at once lets each gain feed the others. The theorem guarantees no cell gets worse.

screens.title: One pattern, many methods
screens.prose: Policy iteration alternates two steps: make the values match the policy, then make the policy greedy for the values. **Generalised policy iteration** is any mix of the two, even rough ones: a few evaluation sweeps, then an improvement. Levels 3 and 4 follow this pattern.
screens.question: Value iteration is generalised policy iteration with how much evaluation between improvements?

options.text: One sweep: each backup evaluates once, then maxes
A full linear solve of the policy each time
options.why: That is policy iteration. Value iteration never solves for a fixed policy.

options.text: None at all: each backup only improves
options.why: Each backup looks one step ahead using the current values: that is one sweep of evaluation.

options.text: Sweeps until the values stop changing at all
options.why: That would be a full evaluation, as in policy iteration.

hints.text: Look at the backup: what does the max act on?
It scores moves with the current values, a one-step evaluation.
Then it takes the best, an improvement.

feedback.correct: One backup per sweep: evaluation and improvement in a single line.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask how much evaluating value iteration does before each max.

explain.text: Value iteration folds one evaluation sweep and an improvement into each backup. Policy iteration evaluates fully. Both converge to the optimal values; they trade cheap steps against few steps.

screens.title: Two answers, one optimum
screens.prose: On the deterministic grid, policy iteration ends with R at row 2 column 1; value iteration's arg-max, which takes the first best of U, R, D, L, says U there. The two disagree in 7 cells, yet their values agree to $10^{-15}$.
screens.question: What do you conclude?

options.text: Both are optimal: in those cells U and R tie
Policy iteration is right; value iteration's arg-max is wrong
options.why: The values agree, and U and R score the same in those cells. Neither is wrong.

options.text: Value iteration is right, as it is the more precise method
options.why: Both reach the optimal values. The difference is only which tied action each picked.

options.text: One of the codes has a bug that needs finding
options.why: Ties are not a bug. Compare policies by whether each action is in the optimal set.

hints.text: Compare the values the two moves lead to.
From row 2 column 1, U and R both lead to cells worth 0.5914.
Equal scores mean either move is optimal.

feedback.correct: They pick different members of the same optimal sets.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check whether the two moves score the same.

byKey.pi: You compared single arg-max choices. In a tie any best action is optimal.

explain.text: In the 7 highlighted cells U and R score exactly the same. Policies should be compared by asking whether every chosen action is in the optimal set, not by equality of one arg-max.

screens.title: Code policy iteration
screens.prose: `evaluate_policy` from l6 is in the editor. Write `policy_iteration(slip, gamma)` from "always U", keeping a cell's action when it ties for best, so the loop cannot flip between tied moves. Then `same_policy`, which accepts two policies when every action of both is a best action.
screens.question: Complete `policy_iteration` and `same_policy`.

widget.how: Submit runs 9 hidden tests with NumPy. Counts and actions must equal ours; values must match within 1e-6.

hints.text: Loop: evaluate, then build a new policy cell by cell.
Keep `policy[s]` if `q[policy[s]] > best - 1e-9`.
Stop when `new == policy`; count every evaluation.

feedback.correct: All pass. On the deterministic grid the two methods' policies differ yet `same_policy` accepts them.
feedback.generic: Some tests fail. Check the tie rule and that the final, unchanged evaluation is counted.

explain.text: Keeping a tied action stops the loop from swapping U and R for ever on the deterministic grid. `same_policy` asks the right question: is every chosen action optimal under these values?

screens.title: A floor more slippery
screens.prose: Raise the slip chance to 0.2 each side, so the intended move succeeds only 6 times in 10. At row 2, column 4, moving U risks a slip R into the pit. Predict what the best action becomes there, then check.
screens.question: With slip 0.2, what is the best move at row 2, column 4?

options.text: L, into the wall
U, still the shortest way to the goal
options.why: U now slips R into the pit with chance 0.2. Each such slip costs −1.04, too much to risk.

options.text: D, away from the pit
options.why: D's slips go L into the wall or R into the pit, so it risks the pit as often as U.

options.text: R, straight at the goal column
options.why: R enters the pit 6 times in 10.

hints.text: Which moves can slip into the pit, column 5 of row 2?
U and D both slip sideways, and one side is the pit.
L bumps the wall; its slips go U and D, away from the pit.

feedback.correct: L: the agent stays put 6 times in 10 and slips U or D otherwise, never into the pit.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check each move's slips.

explain.text: With slip 0.2, L into the wall is worth 0.2255 there: it waits for a safe slip up. U would risk the pit with 0.2. Small changes to the model can flip the policy near danger, so check the policy, not only the values.

screens.title: Policy iteration
screens.prose: Policy iteration: evaluate $v_\pi$ by solving $(\mathbf I - \gamma\mathbf P_\pi)\mathbf v = \mathbf r_\pi$; improve by $\pi'(s) = \arg\max_a \sum_{s'} p\,[r + \gamma v_\pi(s')]$, keeping ties; stop when the policy repeats. With finitely many states and actions it stops after finitely many steps, at an optimal policy.
screens.question: Why must policy iteration stop?

options.text: Each step improves or stops, and there are finitely many policies
The values shrink by a factor $\gamma$ at each step
options.why: That is the contraction behind value iteration. Policy iteration stops because policies never repeat while improving.

options.text: The grid has only 17 states to choose in
options.why: Size sets how long it takes, not whether it stops.

options.text: It picks moves at random until one of them works
options.why: Every step is deterministic: evaluate exactly, then take the best moves.

feedback.correct: No policy can recur while values strictly improve, and there are only $4^{17}$ policies here.
feedback.generic: Count the policies, and use the theorem.

screens.title: Measure, improve, measure again
screens.prose: The quoting rule from l6 is worth £61.31 flat and £57.38 at its limit ($\gamma = 0.95$). At the limit a trader proposes skewing the quotes: earn only £0.50 a step but get back to flat with chance 0.8 instead of 0.5.
screens.question: Using the current values, what is the one-step score of skewing at the limit? Give pounds to 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Score = reward + 0.95 × the average next value.
Next value: $0.8 \times 61.31 + 0.2 \times 57.38$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Score the skew with the values of the current rule.

byKey.current: That is the current value at the limit, to compare against.
byKey.no-disc: You left out the discount on the next value.
byKey.swapped: You swapped the chances: skewing returns to flat with 0.8.

explain.text: Skewing scores £58.00 against £57.38 for one-sided quotes, so improvement switches to skewing. Then the desk re-measures the new rule and asks again: that loop is policy iteration.

ideas: Policy improvement makes a policy greedy for its own values; by the policy improvement theorem no state gets worse.
Policy iteration alternates exact evaluation and improvement. On the slippery grid it reached value iteration's policy in 4 evaluations from "always U".
Optimal policies can tie. Compare policies by whether every chosen action is in the optimal set, and keep the current action on a tie so the loop stops.

formula.name: Policy improvement
formula.note: Then $v_{\pi'} \ge v_\pi$ in every state; equality everywhere means $\pi$ is optimal.

summary.trap: Comparing two policies by one arg-max per cell and reporting a difference where the actions tie.

quiz.prose: Under a policy, a state's current action scores 2.0. Its other actions score 2.4, 1.1 and 2.4.
quiz.question: What does policy improvement do in this state?

options.text: Switches to one of the two actions scoring 2.4
Keeps the current action
options.why: Keeping is right only when the current action ties for best. It scores 2.0, below 2.4.

options.text: Mixes the two best actions at random
options.why: Improvement picks a single best action; either 2.4 will do.

options.text: Stops, since two actions tie
options.why: A tie between two better actions is no reason to stop.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the current score with the best.

explain.text: Improvement picks an action with the best score, 2.4. Any rule for choosing between the two tied ones gives an optimal improvement.

quiz.prose: A policy's improvement leaves every action unchanged.
quiz.question: What does that tell you?

options.text: The policy is optimal: its values satisfy the optimality equation
It is only a local best, and a random restart could beat it
options.why: For a finite MDP a policy greedy for its own values is optimal; there are no local traps.

options.text: Nothing yet: run more evaluations
options.why: Evaluating the same policy again gives the same values and the same greedy step.

options.text: Value iteration would find a better one
options.why: Both methods reach the same optimal values.

feedback.correct: Greedy for its own values means the Bellman optimality equation holds.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about what the max of the backup equals.

explain.text: If $\pi$ is greedy for $v_\pi$, then $v_\pi(s) = \max_a \sum p[r + \gamma v_\pi]$, the optimality equation. So $v_\pi = V^*$.

quiz.prose: On the slippery grid (slip 0.1) the step cost is set to 0, so moving is free.
quiz.question: At row 3, column 5, beside the pit, which move becomes best?

options.text: D, away from the pit: waiting is free
L, the same move as before
options.why: With a step cost L is a fair compromise. With free steps, D into the corner risks nothing and costs nothing.

options.text: U, straight on past the pit
options.why: U enters the pit 8 times in 10.

options.text: R, into the edge of the grid
options.why: R bumps the edge but slips U into the pit one time in ten.

feedback.correct: With free steps, safety wins: D never slips into the pit.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which moves can slip into the pit?

explain.text: D's slips go L and R, neither into the pit, and waiting costs nothing but discounting. Value iteration with step cost 0 picks D there.
